title: ERCOT prices at generator nodes
blurb: Real-Time Market settlement prices at 1,087 ERCOT generator settlement points for one 15-minute interval, 2:45 to 3:00 pm CT on Sunday, November 1, 2026. The Houston load zone settled at $73.66/MWh while North and West Texas sat near $11.
alt: Dark map of Texas with dots at generator locations on a continuous color scale from blue (negative prices) through teal and yellow to red ($170/MWh and up), over faint load zone outlines. North and West Texas dots are teal, near $10; South Texas dots are yellow-green, near $45; dots along the Houston Ship Channel are orange and red, above $100.

title: The Texas pipeline network
blurb: 365,000 miles of pipeline mapped by the Railroad Commission of Texas, 316,000 of them in service, colored by commodity. Gathering lines that collect oil and gas from wells make up 60% of the mileage and form the dense mesh in the Permian Basin and Eagle Ford.
alt: Dark map of Texas covered in a dense web of colored lines: natural gas in blue, crude oil in orange, NGLs in green, refined products in yellow, and CO2 in purple. Abandoned and removed lines appear as thin gray strokes, most visible along the Gulf Coast. The mesh is densest in the Permian Basin, the Eagle Ford, and around Houston.

title: Where America's solar farms are
blurb: 6,611 US solar facilities of 1 MW AC or more, 131.6 GW AC in all, grouped into hexagons by capacity and drawn as their real footprints over satellite imagery as you zoom in. Texas and California each hold about 17% of the capacity. Facilities under 10 MW are 77% of the count but 11% of the capacity.
alt: Satellite globe view of the contiguous United States covered in hexagons colored from dark purple (under 10 MW AC) to pale yellow (1,000 MW AC or more). The brightest hexagons are in the California and Arizona deserts, around Las Vegas, and in West Texas and Houston. Small purple hexagons fill the Northeast, Minnesota, and the Carolinas.

title: Every US power plant
blurb: Every operating US power plant in EIA Form 860M (September 2026), clustered on the map, with each ring showing the cluster's nameplate capacity by fuel. Gas is 41% of the 1,417 GW, while solar is 12% even though half of all plants are solar. Texas has the most battery storage, 19.4 GW to California's 16.5 GW.
alt: Dark globe view of the United States covered in donut-shaped clusters, each labeled with its total capacity, from 296 MW in northern Maine to 221 GW around Indiana and Ohio, with Hawaii's 3.7 GW at the left edge. Ring segments show the fuel mix: mostly coral gas across Texas and the Southeast, blue hydro in the Pacific Northwest, green wind on the Plains, and yellow solar with purple batteries in Southern California.

title: Within sight of a wind turbine
blurb: Where the blade tips of 1,666 wind turbines in Nolan and Taylor counties, Texas, are in line of sight from the ground, out to 25 miles, computed from USGS elevation data with earth curvature. At least one blade tip is in line of sight from 74% of the land within 25 miles of these turbines. Click a turbine to see its own viewshed, banded at 10 and 20 miles.
alt: Tilted 3D satellite view of the rolling ranchland around Sweetwater and Abilene, Texas, with a large rounded patch of color centered on two counties of wind farms. White dots mark 1,666 turbines in long rows along the ridges and mesas. The overlay shades each spot by how many blade tips are in line of sight from it: deep purple on the high ground near the turbine rows, where more than 1,000 tips can be in view, fading through red and orange to pale yellow at the outer edge, about 25 miles from the turbines.

title: The Permian Basin, 1958 and today
blurb: Four 1957–58 Army Map Service topographic sheets around Midland, Texas, which drew each well as a small circle, swiped against satellite imagery and the 447,665 wells on record in the same area today. The map opens on the Kermit and Wink oil fields in Winkler County.
alt: Swipe map split down the middle. On the left, a 1950s Army Map Service topographic sheet of Kermit and Wink, Texas, in pale green with red roads, labeled Winkler County Oil and Gas Field and Wink Oil Field, with hundreds of small open circles marking wells, along with pipelines, pumping stations and oil tanks. On the right, satellite imagery of the same tan ranchland today, crossed by caliche roads and well pads, with thousands of bright cyan dots marking wells.
